title: Respond to a new transfusion reaction
stem: During red-cell transfusion, a client develops new chills, fever and back discomfort. Which actions belong in the immediate reaction response? Select all that apply.
options: Discard the bag and tubing immediately
Give the next unit because the first may simply be cold
Stop the transfusion and promptly assess the client
Notify the appropriate team and follow the reaction investigation protocol
Slow the transfusion until the chills settle
why: The product and administration set may be needed for investigation.
A new unit should not be started before the reaction is assessed.
Further exposure should cease while a possible serious reaction is evaluated.
The event requires coordinated evaluation, sampling and product handling.
Continuing exposure can worsen a serious reaction.
takeaway: Further exposure should cease while a possible serious reaction is evaluated.
learningObjective: Initiate the transfusion-reaction pathway when new systemic symptoms develop during blood administration.

title: Differentiate possible transfusion overload
stem: An older client with heart failure develops breathlessness during transfusion. Which findings particularly support circulatory overload in the differential? Select all that apply.
options: Rising blood pressure and venous congestion
Isolated urticaria with unchanged breathing and pressure
New severe back pain with hypotension and dark urine
A stable mild bruise at a previous venipuncture site
New crackles with increasing oxygen requirement
why: These findings support increased intravascular volume and pressure.
This pattern more strongly suggests an allergic skin reaction.
This combination raises concern for hemolysis rather than isolated overload.
That unchanged local finding does not explain acute respiratory symptoms.
Pulmonary fluid accumulation can impair oxygenation.
takeaway: Pulmonary fluid accumulation can impair oxygenation.
learningObjective: Recognize a circulatory-overload pattern during transfusion while arranging urgent assessment.

title: Report delayed transfusion symptoms
stem: A client is discharged after an uncomplicated transfusion. Which new findings should be reported promptly with mention of the recent transfusion? Select all that apply.
options: The pre-existing mild dry skin remains unchanged
New jaundice or unusually dark urine
Unexpected fever, worsening fatigue or breathlessness
A small unchanged bruise at the venipuncture site
Gradually improving usual activity tolerance
why: An unchanged baseline skin finding does not suggest a delayed reaction.
Delayed hemolysis may become apparent after leaving the facility.
These symptoms warrant assessment and the transfusion history helps guide it.
A stable localized bruise is less concerning than new systemic symptoms.
Functional improvement can reflect the intended benefit of transfusion.
takeaway: Delayed hemolysis may become apparent after leaving the facility.
learningObjective: Include delayed warning symptoms in post-transfusion discharge teaching.

title: Resolve a blood-unit identity discrepancy
stem: A blood unit's compatibility label has an identification number that differs from the client's wristband by one digit. The name matches. What is appropriate?
options: Ask the client to confirm their blood group
Correct the number on the label at the bedside
Stop the verification process and resolve the discrepancy
Use the matching name to approve the unit
why: A remembered blood group cannot replace compatibility and identity checks.
A handwritten correction does not establish the blood bank's intended compatibility.
All required identifiers must agree before exposing the client to the component.
A name match does not resolve a potentially serious identification error.
takeaway: All required identifiers must agree before exposing the client to the component.
learningObjective: Verify concordant client and component identifiers before transfusion.

title: Confirm compatible red-cell tubing fluid
stem: A red-cell unit is ready, but the intended line contains dextrose solution. What should the nurse do?
options: Connect the unit to the existing line because both solutions are clear
Run the dextrose more slowly during transfusion
Use the dextrose only to prime the blood filter
Establish an approved compatible blood-administration setup
why: Appearance does not establish compatibility with red cells.
Lowering the rate does not remove the incompatibility concern.
Priming still exposes cells to the solution when transfusion begins.
Red-cell compatibility requires a suitable solution and tubing plan, commonly normal saline under policy.
takeaway: Red-cell compatibility requires a suitable solution and tubing plan, commonly normal saline under policy.
learningObjective: Use approved compatibility guidance for fluids sharing red-cell administration tubing.

title: Assess a new fever before transfusion
stem: Immediately before a planned nonemergency transfusion, the client's temperature is newly elevated and they report chills. What is appropriate?
options: Assess and report the change before starting the component
Give an antipyretic and begin as soon as the temperature falls
Use yesterday's normal temperature as the baseline
Assume the transfusion will treat the fever because hemoglobin is low
why: A new baseline problem needs review and can complicate recognition of a reaction.
Suppressing fever does not explain the new symptoms or complete the assessment.
The current condition is the relevant comparison for transfusion monitoring.
Red-cell replacement does not establish treatment of the fever's cause.
takeaway: A new baseline problem needs review and can complicate recognition of a reaction.
learningObjective: Establish and communicate a changed baseline before initiating a prescribed blood component.

title: Evaluate a platelet transfusion response
stem: A client with thrombocytopenia receives prescribed platelets. Which observations help assess the intended response? Select all that apply.
options: Reduced mucosal oozing with no new bleeding
A larger hemoglobin rise as the principal expected effect
Improved appetite as the only follow-up measure
Normal temperature alone after the component ends
The post-transfusion platelet result reviewed at the ordered time
why: Clinical hemostasis provides meaningful information beyond the count.
Platelets are not primarily given to increase red-cell mass.
Appetite does not directly assess platelet or bleeding response.
Absence of fever is reassuring for safety but does not establish hemostatic effectiveness.
An appropriately timed count helps evaluate the increment.
takeaway: An appropriately timed count helps evaluate the increment.
learningObjective: Use platelet and bleeding findings to evaluate platelet-component therapy.

title: Explain a prescribed plasma component
stem: A client with a documented clotting-factor deficiency is prescribed plasma and asks why red cells are not being used instead. What explanation is most accurate?
options: Plasma mainly increases platelet production immediately
The purpose is solely to increase fluid intake
Plasma provides clotting factors for the identified problem
Red cells and plasma supply the same coagulation components
why: Plasma does not directly produce an immediate platelet increment.
Using a blood component requires an indication beyond routine hydration.
Component selection is based on the deficient function being treated.
They have different principal therapeutic roles.
takeaway: Component selection is based on the deficient function being treated.
learningObjective: Distinguish clotting-factor replacement from red-cell or platelet replacement.

title: Manage an unexpected PN interruption
stem: A client's continuous high-dextrose parenteral nutrition stops because the line fails. Replacement access is being arranged. What is appropriate?
options: Use the next routine meal glucose time for reassessment
Substitute the same volume of saline as nutritional replacement
Restart later at twice the previous rate to catch up
Check glucose and implement the ordered interruption plan
why: Unexpected interruption can require earlier glucose assessment.
Saline does not provide the interrupted glucose or nutrients.
Accelerated delivery can create metabolic and fluid complications.
An abrupt change in glucose delivery may require monitored support until nutrition resumes.
takeaway: An abrupt change in glucose delivery may require monitored support until nutrition resumes.
learningObjective: Assess glucose and activate the prescribed contingency plan when continuous PN stops unexpectedly.

title: Monitor a new PN regimen
stem: A malnourished client begins prescribed PN. Which monitoring domains are relevant? Select all that apply.
options: Glucose and ordered electrolyte trends
Weight, fluid balance and signs of congestion
Catheter site and systemic infection symptoms
Daily oral appetite as the sole response measure
Stopping all laboratory checks after the first tolerated bag
why: PN can change glucose and electrolyte balance, especially early in therapy.
The infused volume must be evaluated against tolerance and nutritional goals.
Vascular access creates an additional route for infection.
Appetite does not evaluate intravenous nutrient delivery or its complications.
Early tolerance does not establish ongoing metabolic stability.
takeaway: PN can change glucose and electrolyte balance, especially early in therapy.
learningObjective: Select metabolic, fluid and access assessments after parenteral nutrition is initiated.

title: Verify central PN access requirements
stem: A PN bag is labelled for central administration, but only a peripheral cannula is currently usable. What is appropriate?
options: Dilute the bag at the bedside to make it peripheral
Clarify access or an alternative formulation before infusion
Use the peripheral cannula because it flushes easily
Run the central formulation slowly through the peripheral line
why: Unapproved dilution compromises formulation and compounding safety.
A central formulation may be unsuitable for peripheral veins.
Patency does not establish that the formulation is suitable for that vessel.
A slower rate does not necessarily make its concentration appropriate.
takeaway: A central formulation may be unsuitable for peripheral veins.
learningObjective: Match a central PN formulation to a verified appropriate vascular-access route.

title: Protect a dedicated PN lumen
stem: A client has a designated central-lumen PN infusion and another usable lumen. Which practices support safe delivery? Select all that apply.
options: Check any proposed co-infusion with an approved resource
Add routine medicines to the PN bag during bedside administration
Use a clear appearance as proof that mixed medicines are compatible
Disconnect the PN frequently for convenience despite other access
Use the designated lumen according to the PN plan
why: PN contains multiple constituents and compatibility cannot be assumed.
Unapproved additions can affect stability, compatibility and dose accuracy.
Some incompatibilities or stability problems are not visually apparent.
Repeated manipulation adds avoidable interruption and contamination opportunities.
Dedicated access helps reduce incompatible mixing and unnecessary manipulation.
takeaway: Dedicated access helps reduce incompatible mixing and unnecessary manipulation.
learningObjective: Limit incompatibility and unnecessary manipulation of the parenteral-nutrition pathway.

title: Recognize refeeding-associated electrolyte decline
stem: A severely malnourished client starts nutrition support and develops weakness with a marked fall in phosphate. What is appropriate?
options: Increase nutrition faster because weakness indicates inadequate calories
Judge progress from calorie delivery alone
Treat the phosphate result as unrelated because nutrition is intravenous
Report possible refeeding complications and review the prescribed progression
why: Rapid advancement may worsen the underlying electrolyte shifts.
Calorie delivery does not establish metabolic tolerance.
Refeeding shifts can occur with parenteral as well as enteral intake.
Insulin-driven shifts after feeding can produce dangerous electrolyte depletion.
takeaway: Insulin-driven shifts after feeding can produce dangerous electrolyte depletion.
learningObjective: Escalate new phosphate depletion and weakness after nutrition is restarted in severe malnutrition.

title: Explain prescribed isotonic volume replacement
stem: A client with vomiting and circulatory volume depletion is prescribed an isotonic crystalloid. What is the principal immediate treatment goal?
options: Restore extracellular circulating volume and perfusion
Provide complete daily calorie and protein requirements
Produce rapid correction of every electrolyte deficit
Deliver free water as the primary intracellular replacement
why: The solution supports volume replacement when intravascular filling is reduced.
Isotonic crystalloid is not complete nutritional support.
Individual deficits may require additional prescribed treatment.
An isotonic solution is chosen for extracellular volume support rather than primarily free-water replacement.
takeaway: The solution supports volume replacement when intravascular filling is reduced.
learningObjective: Connect an isotonic crystalloid prescription with treatment of extracellular volume depletion.

title: Monitor prescribed hypertonic saline
stem: A client receives hypertonic saline under a specific correction protocol. Which checks are relevant? Select all that apply.
options: Verify the ordered concentration and programmed rate
Monitor sodium trends and neurological status at the ordered intervals
Adjust the rate based on thirst between blood tests
Use a single normal pressure as evidence monitoring can stop
Increase the rate whenever confusion persists
why: A concentration or rate error can cause rapid unintended sodium changes.
Both the correction rate and clinical response inform ongoing safety.
Thirst alone cannot guide controlled sodium correction.
Blood pressure does not establish sodium or neurological stability.
Persistent symptoms require review rather than an independent infusion increase.
takeaway: A concentration or rate error can cause rapid unintended sodium changes.
learningObjective: Apply controlled-rate and neurological monitoring during authorized hypertonic saline treatment.

title: Assess urine output before potassium replacement
stem: A client prescribed IV potassium has newly very low urine output and rising creatinine. The nurse has not yet started the infusion. What is appropriate?
options: Use a larger fluid volume as the sole adjustment
Infuse faster so a follow-up level can be obtained sooner
Report the renal change and clarify the replacement plan
Start because potassium was low on yesterday's sample
why: Dilution changes concentration but does not remove the delivered potassium load.
Faster delivery can increase cardiac risk and is not an authorized response.
Reduced potassium elimination can change the safety of a previously intended dose.
The current renal condition and potassium result need review.
takeaway: Reduced potassium elimination can change the safety of a previously intended dose.
learningObjective: Recognize reduced potassium elimination as relevant before a replacement infusion.

title: Recognize magnesium toxicity
stem: A client receiving prescribed magnesium sulfate has slow respirations, absent deep-tendon reflexes and falling urine output. What should the competent nurse do?
options: Continue while waiting for the next routine magnesium level
Give a sedative because the client appears uncomfortable
Reposition the client and judge safety by blood pressure alone
Stop the infusion and activate the toxicity protocol
why: Clinical toxicity requires action before a routine laboratory interval.
Additional depression may worsen respiratory compromise.
Position and pressure do not resolve the respiratory and reflex findings.
Reduced elimination with neuromuscular depression suggests potentially serious magnesium toxicity.
takeaway: Reduced elimination with neuromuscular depression suggests potentially serious magnesium toxicity.
learningObjective: Escalate respiratory depression and loss of reflexes during magnesium sulfate infusion.

title: Distinguish seizure prophylaxis from pressure control
stem: A client with severe preeclampsia receives magnesium sulfate and a separate antihypertensive. They ask why both are needed. What is best?
options: They address seizure risk and high blood pressure respectively
The antihypertensive is needed only if magnesium causes a fever
The two medicines are interchangeable if a dose is delayed
Magnesium is being used primarily to remove excess body fluid
why: Magnesium's principal role here is seizure prevention rather than reliable pressure control.
Its indication is the hypertension, not a magnesium-related fever.
They have different therapeutic purposes and cannot simply substitute for each other.
That does not explain its anticonvulsant role in this setting.
takeaway: Magnesium's principal role here is seizure prevention rather than reliable pressure control.
learningObjective: Explain why magnesium and a separate antihypertensive may both be prescribed in severe preeclampsia.

title: Review a possibly contaminated heparin sample
stem: A heparin-monitoring blood sample drawn through the lumen infusing heparin is unexpectedly very high. The client has no new bleeding. What is appropriate?
options: Use the prior day's value for all current dose decisions
Report the sampling route and obtain protocol guidance for repeat testing
Assume the value accurately reflects systemic anticoagulation
Ignore the result because no bleeding is visible
why: An old result cannot replace a valid current measurement.
Heparin contamination may distort the result and needs timely clarification.
The collection route may have introduced additional heparin into the specimen.
A high result still needs prompt resolution and clinical assessment.
takeaway: Heparin contamination may distort the result and needs timely clarification.
learningObjective: Consider sampling contamination before interpreting an unexpected anticoagulation result.

title: Recognize an unexpectedly high neuraxial block
stem: A trained nurse monitoring prescribed epidural analgesia notes rapidly increasing leg heaviness, low pressure and difficulty taking a deep breath. What is appropriate?
options: Increase the analgesic because heaviness suggests unresolved pain
Wait for routine catheter dressing care before notifying the team
Initiate the emergency epidural assessment protocol and call anesthesia
Encourage mobilization to test the degree of weakness
why: More local anesthetic may worsen an excessive block.
The acute physiological changes require immediate review.
The pattern may indicate excessive block with respiratory and circulatory effects.
Movement is unsafe during possible hemodynamic and motor compromise.
takeaway: The pattern may indicate excessive block with respiratory and circulatory effects.
learningObjective: Escalate spreading weakness and breathing difficulty during epidural analgesia.

title: Recognize systemic local-anesthetic toxicity
stem: During a local-anesthetic procedure, a client develops ringing ears, metallic taste and slurred speech. Which responses are appropriate? Select all that apply.
options: Continue the procedure until the planned dose is complete
Treat the symptoms solely as pre-procedure anxiety
Alert the procedural team and stop further anesthetic administration
Prepare to support airway, circulation and the emergency protocol
Reassure that these symptoms confirm the intended local numbness
why: Additional exposure can worsen toxicity.
The temporal relationship and characteristic symptoms require a toxicity assessment.
The symptoms may be early systemic toxicity before seizures or cardiac effects.
Rapid progression is possible, so resuscitation readiness is important.
They are systemic neurological effects rather than merely local anesthesia.
takeaway: The symptoms may be early systemic toxicity before seizures or cardiac effects.
learningObjective: Respond to early neurological warning symptoms during local-anesthetic administration.

title: Respond to an open central-line system
stem: A central-line connection opens and the client develops sudden dyspnea and chest discomfort. What should the nurse do first?
options: Occlude the open system and activate emergency assessment
Flush the open line to clear any visible bubbles
Replace the connector before assessing the new symptoms
Check whether the dressing date is current before intervening
why: Stopping further air entry addresses a possible air-embolism mechanism while help is obtained.
Flushing can introduce additional air into the circulation.
Restoring hardware alone does not address the acute respiratory event.
Routine dressing information does not take priority over an open line and deterioration.
takeaway: Stopping further air entry addresses a possible air-embolism mechanism while help is obtained.
learningObjective: Stop further air entry and escalate sudden symptoms after central-line disconnection.

title: Account for medicine remaining in tubing
stem: A small-volume IV medicine has left the bag, but medication-containing fluid remains in the tubing. A compatible flush volume and rate are prescribed. What should the nurse do?
options: Increase the next dose to replace the estimated residual
Complete the prescribed flush at the specified rate
Disconnect immediately because the medication bag is empty
Flush rapidly to finish the medication round
why: Dose compensation is unprescribed and the residual should be managed now.
This delivers the residual medicine without an unintended rapid bolus.
An empty bag does not mean the full intended dose has reached the client.
Rapid flushing can deliver residual medicine faster than prescribed.
takeaway: This delivers the residual medicine without an unintended rapid bolus.
learningObjective: Use the prescribed compatible flush plan to deliver residual medicine safely after a small-volume infusion.

title: Maintain blood integrity when transfusion is delayed
stem: A nonemergency transfusion is postponed after the blood unit arrives on the unit. What should the nurse do?
options: Keep it at the bedside until the next routine round
Ask a family member to hold the unit cool during the delay
Contact the blood bank and follow the return/storage policy
Place the unit in the medication refrigerator
why: Uncontrolled delay may exceed allowable handling limits.
Improvised cooling does not preserve a validated storage process.
Component integrity depends on approved handling and time-temperature limits.
An unapproved refrigerator may not maintain validated blood-storage conditions.
takeaway: Component integrity depends on approved handling and time-temperature limits.
learningObjective: Follow blood-bank time and storage requirements when an issued component cannot be started.

title: Limit injection-site bruising
stem: A client learning prescribed subcutaneous enoxaparin rubs the injection site vigorously afterward. What correction is most useful?
options: Massage longer until the lump disappears
Give the next dose into the same bruised area
Reduce the next dose according to bruise size
Avoid rubbing and use gentle pressure if needed
why: More massage can add trauma rather than improve safe absorption.
Repeated injection into injured tissue can worsen local damage.
Bruise size alone does not authorize a dose change.
Rubbing increases tissue trauma and can worsen local bruising.
takeaway: Rubbing increases tissue trauma and can worsen local bruising.
learningObjective: Apply product-specific subcutaneous anticoagulant technique and avoid unnecessary tissue trauma.
